## Exercise 1: Deduce Quarto features

Check out the appearance and contents of this document. Thoughts?

It looks pretty well-formatted, it had a very good information with it's own code chunks and the types of questions it has in document. 

In the toolbar at the top of this document, **Render** the .qmd file into a .html file. Where is this file stored? Thoughts about its appearance / contents? Can you edit it?

The file is stored in ICA folder and it nicely formatted with the content appearing on the website. I can edit the document from here but not the actual webpage itself. It displays the changes between them once I was able to get the changes in there. 

Toggling between the .qmd and .html files, explain the purpose of the following features in the .qmd file:        

`*`
This one word to italic

`**`
This one changes the bolden the words and make it title-like

`#`
This one make a comment in the code in rchunk. 

`-`
This one makes a bullet points like little notes in the webpage.  

`\`
It creates white space in the code that trnasfer over to the html page. 

`![](url)`
it creates a weblink within the code to be usable.

## Exercise 3: Chunks

Quarto isn't a mind reader -- we must distinguish R code from text.
We do so by putting code inside an **R chunk**:

```{r}
seq()
```

- Put the `seq()` code in the chunk.
- Press the green arrow in the top right of the chunk. What happens in the qmd?
- Render. What appears in the html: R code, output, or both?

It runs in the qmd and outputs an answer. 

It shows the rcode chunk and the drop down of the computer itself with the output appearing in a cleaner way compared to the qmd file.

## Exercise 6: Comments

Run the chunk below.
Notice that R ignores anything in a line starting with a pound sign (`#`).
If we took the `#` away we'd get an error!

```{r}
# This is a comment
4 + 5
```

We'll utilize this feature to **comment our code**, i.e. leave short notes about what our code is doing.
Below, replace the `???` with an appropriate comment.

```{r}
# This chunk of code converts the temperature in celsius into fahrenheit temperature. 
temperature_c <- 10
temperature_f <- temperature_c * 9/5 + 32
temperature_f
```
